Basis: Non-native English speaker who works short promos; his mic value is comic, chiefly the Alpha Academy crowd call-and-response and comedy bits rather than long speeches.

Little written about her mic work specifically; her NXT/WWE character as Alba Fyre and the Unholy Union with Isla Dawn has been carried by eerie, sparse segments and vignettes more than long talking promos, so she is placed around her charisma with strength in produced and physical segments.

The second voice of the Street Profits; Montez Ford usually leads their promos and Heyman's 'underrated talkers' remark covered both. Dawkins is relaxed and likeable, best in the team's party-and-dance crowd bits and backstage comedy. Little has been written about him as a talker on his own.

Non-native English speaker who works short, broken-English or Japanese-language promos that land on intensity and odd comedy; strongest in produced mask/mist material and when the talking turns physical.
Masked high-flyer who rarely carries promos; lighter material came in the Fraxiom tag team. Little specific promo coverage found, so values sit near charisma.
Came up as the hype-woman of Hit Row, rapping and working the crowd in-ring; no specific critical reviews of her promos found, so values sit near her charisma with crowd work as the strength.
A dependable heat-drawing heel talker (King Corbin, Happy Corbin) whose promos were functional rather than memorable; the 'says little' loner gimmick here lowers the free-talking side.
Her 2020 'role model' heel run and Damage CTRL leadership are widely credited as a mic breakthrough (whiny, quick, self-aware); the 2024 face turn showed she can carry sincere material too.
'The Man' run was built on her own unscripted-feeling social-media and live promos; widely ranked among the best talkers of her era, equally convincing as defiant face and smug heel.
Reviews are mixed: PWTorch called one promo her shakiest and fans describe her as a bit stiff, while her emotional segments (e.g. with Naomi) land; presence and crowd connection outrun her talking.

Presented on intensity and in-ring brutality; her mic time is short post-match statements and nobody has assessed her delivery in any depth. Kept near her low charisma, and her best setting is physical.

Built her AEW reputation on the produced Toni Storm storyline (vignettes, the kiss, the shoe attack) more than on long live promos; little specific critique of her mic work found, so figures stay near charisma.
Recent NXT signee (Swipe Right, Vanity Project); a May 2026 review said he still needed a character. Judged mainly from his vain-heel gimmick.
Long seen as an uncomfortable talker whose promos are intense, Steiner-style shouting; reviewers say he improved markedly in his 2025 feud with CM Punk. His strength is the explosion, not the words.

Kevin Nash praised him for changing his delivery on the fly when a 'what' chant started, and he is quick-witted on social media. Otherwise he is booked as a monster who talks little, so his strength is in physical segments.
The 2011 'Pipebomb' and his Chicago returns are canonical; consensus places him among the best live talkers of his era, worked mostly off bullet points rather than scripts.
Primarily a worker; promos are earnest and short, with the Poison Pixie and family-themed material done mostly through produced segments. Little specific promo criticism found.

Regarded as one of NXT's best talkers; says he works from bullet points and uses mostly his own words; his promo explaining the turn on Trick Williams was singled out as the most important of his career.

The Alpha Academy betrayal of Otis and his feud with Sami Zayn showed a convincing, smug heel talker. His comedy comes through produced Academy vignettes more than off-the-cuff wit. Better scripted than improvised.
Commanding ring presence and convincing entitled-heel material, but frequently critiqued as rehearsed and over-long when off script.
Widely praised as one of WWE's best comedy heels (the entitled 'Karen' who demands a manager); excels at funny, petty material but is rarely used in serious registers.

Widely ranked among the best talkers of his era (the Kenny Omega promo is a common pick for best modern promo); he says he workshops and focus-groups his material, and criticism centres on length and 'Shakespearean' polish - a prepared, delivered speaker more than an ad-libber.

Her heel turn promo was praised by PWTorch for its ease and expressions, and her title-in-the-trash moment echoed Madusa's belt toss. Critics credit her with a natural snotty heel voice, though she leans on borrowed lines (Punk, AJ Lee).
Little direct critique found; judged from her deadpan backstage work in Damage CTRL and the 2019 NXT heel turn, with values kept near her charisma.
Solid, deep-voiced serious talker from the Judgment Day period and his title run; dependable rather than standout, strongest when menacing.

Known for self-made black-and-white vignettes and soft-spoken sincerity; critics note big improvement in his talking, while Cornette has called his promos flat. Best in produced pieces and quiet delivery, not crowd-led ring promos.

The 'Dirty Dom' character draws boos loud enough to drown his promos, and he works them by lowering the mic and waiting. Peers including Triple H praise him; critics like Russo still fault his delivery. Elite at drawing heat as a cowardly heel, less proven outside that note.
Widely praised bitter-heel run of 2024 against CM Punk and Rollins, with sharp live and social-media material; earlier face run showed a sincere inspirational register.
Rarely featured on the mic; his poker-player gimmick is mostly shown in short backstage and produced bits. Little found; kept near his low charisma.
SI notes he 'has never been viewed as a top promo' though his mic work has improved, with his best promos resting on authenticity; an in-ring worker first.
Mostly a valet/enforcer for Legado del Fantasma, with little featured mic work; she reportedly earned the role from a promo-class performance. Kept near her low charisma.
Rarely the talker in the Viking Raiders; his work is produced Viking vignettes and comedy bits plus brawling, with little standalone mic work.
Long regarded as a strong talker since the indies and AEW, known for self-produced vignettes and an 'All Ego' heel act that is both smug and comic.

By his own account promos were a steep curve in WWE and still make him nervous; fans and Freddie Prinze Jr. say they improved a lot in the Judgment Day era. His charisma is carried by presence and the Demon's produced spectacle more than by talking.

A veteran who is solid on the mic rather than a standout; his smug heel run as TNA World Champion ('I bathe in your tears') suits the Arrogant register. Fans describe him as able to hold his own without being especially charismatic.
In Imperium Gunther and Kaiser did most of the talking; his persona is carried by dancing, posture and short accented lines. Nothing specific found on his promos.
Has said her English was beginner level on arrival and she takes classes to learn to cut a 'proper' promo; works through presence, violence and produced material.

Consistently described as obnoxiously entertaining and strong on the mic, compared with MJF and The Miz; trusted to host his own talk show segment (The Grayson Waller Effect) and quick at needling opponents and crowds.

Widely praised (Cornette, Disco Inferno, Freddie Prinze Jr.) for measured, quotable, cold promos in a second language. He is scripted and deliberate rather than spontaneous, and does not play to the crowd. His strength is out of proportion to his modest charisma figure.
His AEW world-title story and the Swerve Strickland feud (including the home-invasion segment) are noted for raw, sincere promos; also funny in Being the Elite material.
Known for intense, emotional delivery in NXT UK/NXT, but rarely given long promo time and works in his second language; fans note his mic work has seldom been tested.

Her strongest material has been occult vignettes (ouija board, tarot) from NXT UK on and the largely wordless menace of the Unholy Union; no specific reviews of her live promos found, so talking values sit below her charisma.
Ivar's comedy is physical and produced: carpool-karaoke and 'Viking Experience' bits, and a big man's athletic clowning. Erik shares the talking. Little exists on him as a solo talker.
Presented as a silent, intense physical presence in Diamond Mine and American Made; very little mic work to judge.
Limited English; Dakota Kai and Damage CTRL spoke for her for long stretches. Her connection with crowds comes from her work, not the microphone.
Leads the Vanity Project in NXT/EVOLVE as a vain heel; no specific assessments of his promos found, so placed near his charisma.

Once his weakest point by his own account, the mic is now a strength: PWTorch notes an intense cadence and menacing expressions, and WhatCulture says he balances shouting with a measured style. He is best unscripted and 'as himself'. Teddy Long thinks scripted lines suit him less.
Has said she had to get more comfortable on the mic; her 2025 NXT-champion heel promos were serviceable and leaned on smugness. Kept close to her charisma.
Strong physical presence and well-produced entrances and vignettes; live mic work is generally viewed as stiff and short.
Won Women's Promo of the Year at the 2024 NXT Year-End Awards and is described as a strong crowd worker with charisma.
Opinions conflict: she is very popular and comes across natural and blunt, while Konnan says she 'can't cut a promo'. Her best work is physical, and she has said her actions do the talking.
Says he disliked promos on the indies and is still working on them, with advice from Heyman; his strength is energy and crowd connection rather than words.
Enormous crowd connection and artistic produced material, but his talking promos are commonly seen as soft-spoken and meandering.

Critics (Konnan, Russo and others) say his talking relies on catchphrases and fumbles, but the 'YEET' call-and-response makes him one of the best crowd-led acts in WWE; his Bloodline-era emotional segments landed.

Half of the Usos, one of the most crowd-connected acts of their era, with a loose hip-hop cadence and strong call-and-response. He did heavy Bloodline dramatic work too, though Jey usually took the more emotional beats.
Celebrated for unscripted, gritty AEW and indie promos and openly critical of WWE's scripted lines; at his best when the talk turns into violence.
Earnest, competent talker from her TNA Knockouts title runs; not noted as a standout promo. Little specific coverage found.
Non-native English speaker who works short promos; her appeal is expressive and visual (pirate-princess act, crowd singalongs) rather than verbal. No specific promo reviews found.
An NXT/AAA midcarder with little featured mic work; no promo assessments were found. Kept near her charisma.
Former American Ninja Warrior athlete whose presentation is mostly in-ring; little notable mic work found.
Celebrated presence in Japan (Rainmaker money drops, Japanese promos), but works in limited English and in AEW has largely had Don Callis speak for him.
Reviewers call her a good talker but note she rarely varies her vocal inflection ('less is more'); one PWTorch column marked a 2026 promo a miss despite good content.

Known for goofy, gamer-humour promos, a cocky 'Cleaner' heel voice, and earnest emotional sit-downs (the Golden Lovers, returning from illness). His best produced work is Being The Elite and cinematic segments. Promos are good, but less celebrated than his matches.
Regarded as one of WWE's most complete talkers: blunt, quotable, funny or furious off the cuff, and comfortable brawling inside segments (the KO Show).
Comedy and energy as part of the New Day; his best-remembered solo promos are the emotional KofiMania segments in 2019.
Says herself she feels awkward on the microphone and has had little promo time; her memorable mic moments are physical or offbeat (squatting Renee Paquette).
Consensus as one of the best live talkers in the business: catchphrases, rhythm, and total command of call-and-response ('YEAH!'). Rarely asked to do vulnerable or emotional material.
Reviewers have called mic work his weak spot, though a 2025 review credited newfound confidence and heel promo ability; his main asset is crowd energy.
Her 2024 'Revenge Tour' heel run against Rhea Ripley was built on obsessive, emotional promos and produced segments, marking a clear step up on the mic.

A natural camera presence who draws real heat, but he has said he is not comfortable on the mic, has been accused of repetition and was seen with notes during a promo; produced and physical segments are his strength.
Tommy Dreamer singled out her emotional NXT promo about her mother's illness. Otherwise her mic work is short MMA-style threats, and her flashy entrance and dancing do much of the crowd work.
Gunther publicly called him 'underratedly charismatic' and a really good talker; his theatrical, condescending Imperium mouthpiece promos drew positive fan reaction.
Understated, sincere talker; promos are short and competent rather than memorable. Little specific coverage found.
Widely regarded as the best heel talker of his generation; exceptionally quick off the cuff and able to switch to emotional, worked-shoot material (e.g. the CM Punk feud).

His 'Broken/Woken' character and the cinematic Final Deletion are landmark produced segments. He moves between absurd comedy, sinister and sincere veteran registers, and is strongest on produced material.
Has described her early promos as nervous and 'cringey' and faced heavy criticism while green; improved through Alpha Academy and produced Maximum Male Models material.
Very strong star presence and heavily produced 'CEO' persona; occasional flubbed or over-rehearsed lines keep her raw mic figures below her aura.
Has said she is a horrible actress and that promos are the hardest part of wrestling for her; a physical, no-nonsense worker.
Paul Heyman called the Street Profits the most underrated talkers in WWE, and The Rock has compared Ford's promo style to his own. He is loud, rhythmic and crowd-driven, best live in the ring.
Described as intense and methodical on the mic; a 2026 review praised his vitriol, though crowds have sometimes chanted over him.
Regarded as a thoughtful storyteller on the mic: emotional face promos and a theatrical, self-righteous political-campaign heel act in NXT and the indies.
A high-flyer given little promo time; no specific assessments of his mic work found, so placed near his charisma.

Her 2024 Queen run drew strong heat, and outlets credit Heyman-era improvement. Cornette repeatedly calls her delivery memorized and monotone. Her heat comes from presence and physicality more than words, so the figures sit below her 92 charisma.
Long-time 'show-off' character with competent, sometimes cheesy scripted WWE promos; also a stand-up comedian, and more freewheeling in TNA.
Few words with great weight; Bully Ray praised a return promo that brought the crowd to its feet. Has said he code-switches his accent for effect.
His act is physical and expressive comedy (the Mandy Rose romance, the caterpillar, luchador skits) rather than talking; critics call the comedy segments gold and his speech 'jabbering'.

His appeal is the 'Cero Miedo' call-and-response, his gestures and his cinematic entrance rather than long promos. Speeches are short and bilingual, like his emotional WWE debut. Very strong at crowd work and physical segments, limited on extended scripted English.
No specific promo critique found; mostly a physical heel who has talked as Chelsea Green's partner. Kept near charisma.
The 'Viper' style is quiet, deliberate menace, at its best in slow or sit-down promos and segments that end in an RKO; less convincing in comedy or high-energy material.
A powerhouse whose segments lean on physicality; no specific reviews of her promos found, so values sit at or below her charisma.

Rarely speaks, and only briefly, in Spanish or limited English; his connection with the crowd comes from his flying and his reactions. No promo assessments were found, so the figures follow his gimmick.
Her presence and crowd connection ('Mami' chants) outstrip her words; serviceable-to-good talker who dominates segments physically.
Known since AEW as a quick, cocky talker who held his own with Edge; Jonathan Coachman says delivery still needs work, and a musical-style NXT segment was poorly received.
Part of Jackson Drake's Vanity Project; only short social-media promos found, no critical assessment, so placed near his charisma.

Long criticised as a weak talker in WWE (Cornette, his own 'can't cut a promo' joke). His AEW heel run drew better reviews, especially a backstage segment, so he is better as a smug heel than as a sincere face.
The Tribal Chief run (sit-down Bloodline segments, 'Acknowledge me') is regarded as elite quiet-menace work; his earlier scripted babyface promos were widely panned, showing limited range.
Grew from a sincere crowd-favourite underdog into a convincing whiny 'Prodigy' heel; equally solid in either alignment.
Began with Lana as his mouthpiece as a menacing heel, then was called the funniest man in WWE for the ironic 'Rusev Day' act; accent and short promos keep his scripted delivery ordinary.

The Honorary Uce storyline and Royal Rumble 2023 turn are regarded as some of WWE's best TV in a decade. The Montreal SmackDown promo, which the crowd took over, showed his emotional work. Wide range, from comic heel conspiracy to sincere babyface.
Consistently ranked among the best mic workers; his calm, threatening delivery (e.g. the 2017 Brock Lesnar feud) is the template for quiet menace.
Among the best talkers of his era: 'Visionary' heel theatrics, the 2023 CM Punk promos and stadium-scale crowd work; occasionally criticised as over the top.
Rarely praised for mic work; she favours an understated 'just talk' style she says avoids trying too hard, which suits quiet, cold threat more than crowd-led promos.

The real Sheamus is a solid, often funny talker: the Bar comedy, his banger bits, and his heel arrogance. His best segments turn into brawls. The 'Never Speaks' dark persona here doesn't match his record.
Limited English; charisma comes through mannerisms, entrance and produced pieces (Japanese-language promos, the 2023 Rollins feud) rather than talking.
Strong crowd-interaction energy (the tank and the howl) and a fun produced persona; sit-down and long talking promos are less valued.
Says character work has been the hardest part of wrestling for her and angry promos in particular; her sunny surfer persona carries her with crowds.

Effective as a silent enforcer. As Tribal Chief he was criticised (Matt Morgan, Cornette, Last Word on Sports) for flat, borrowed cadence and leaning on Heyman, though Russo noted improvement. Best in stares, sit-downs and physical segments.
Has said English promos are hard because she thinks in Spanish and translates; strong in Spanish and with crowds, so she leans on presence over words.
Won Fightful's 2023 Best Individual Promo for the Hangman Page feud ('Whose house?'); praised for cool, menacing delivery that rises above the material.
Works as a largely silent giant enforcer; little to no promo record, so talking values are low and presence/physicality carry him.

In WWE he was booked to talk very little, letting his gestures, shushing and 'yeyeye' taunts work the crowd while Solo talked. His first-words promo got a mixed reception. Strongest in attacks and brawls.
Nothing specific found on her promos; judged from the comeback-underdog character with values near her charisma.
Loud, high-energy Chase U comedy character; nothing specific found on her mic skills, so judged from the persona and charisma.

Huge crowd reactions and a strong character; Paul Heyman praised her holding her own in a promo battle with Becky Lynch and she handled an off-script exchange with Charlotte Flair, though veterans like Russo and Mantell have criticised her talking.
Her 'Timeless' character is praised as one of the best in wrestling (Khan, Ospreay, Booker T, RJ City), with old-Hollywood vignettes and committed deadpan delivery. Some fans feel it has gone stale.
Fully committed to the mob-boss 'Don' character and praised for playing it, but the act is accent and script driven, with little improvised work.
Self-described trash talker whose crowd-driven 'Whoop That Trick' chant is a call-and-response weapon; called his Undertaker promo some of his riskiest work.
Green and rarely trusted on the microphone (Robert Stone did much of the talking in their pairing); placed at the roster's floor in line with his charisma.

He admits he has 'never been a good promo', citing ADHD and dyslexia, but has improved with regular TV time. He is at his best cheeky, emotional and unscripted, and his All In entrance package was a highlight.
Green NXT performer who is popular with crowds but has done little notable solo mic work; low-confidence judgement from her gimmick.
Quick, nerdy comedy as part of the New Day and UpUpDownDown; more convincing in jokes than in serious singles material.
A power wrestler with little promo record found; reviews mention her struggling to draw heat. Values at or below her charisma, with physicality the strength.
Praised backstage and by peers (The Miz, McMahon) as a mouthpiece manager for Andrade and Legado. She says WWE rarely let her talk as a babyface, so her strength is the fast, sharp heel register.
Says she has always had a hard time with promos, and Bully Ray called her main-roster promos forced and memorised; her strength is physical work.
